prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock rests on one simple, surprising idea: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts the two clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held without disturbing the transition. That turns atomic spectroscopy into a fractional-uncertainty regime near 1e-18, where the theory-experiment comparison is the whole point. Independent groups (Tokyo/RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) have reproduced and leapfrogged each other, so the result does not depend on a single measurement. It is already used to see the gravitational redshift over millimetres, to constrain variation of fundamental constants and dark-matter couplings, and to prepare a redefinition of the second. Attribution is unusually clean: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstrations, Ye for pushing accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the record. It is distinct from the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped ions. It also speaks to where precision measurement can reveal new physics, which I value above technological motivation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the work could be read as an incremental, if brilliant, refinement of optical frequency standards already honoured through the comb (2005) and ion-clock work (2012), rather than a discovery of something new in nature. A second reservation is attribution at the margin: Ludlow, Oates and colleagues at NIST, Takamoto, Lemonde and Hinkley contributed to the decisive demonstrations, and a two-name prize leaves them out. Some of the most exciting applications, such as clock-based gravitational-wave or dark-matter searches and the redefinition of the second itself, are still prospective.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a textbook new measurement capability that opens further science, with Katori and Ye as a coherent pair, and notes that the priority split between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstrations is recalled from memory.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and the pair. I would sharpen the priority point: Katori's proposal is the conceptual step and his group's early strontium lattice work is the first demonstration, while Ye's group made the accuracy and many-body-clock demonstration that made the world take the idea seriously. Our two-name citation should therefore be worded around the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and not around the comb. I am less confident than you that the NIST strontium and Lemonde contributions can be set aside, and I think we should ask for a check of that record before the final ballot.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B031 only eighth, accepting that Katori and Ye are the natural pair and the clocks are mature, but pointing to the earlier comb recognition and the contributions of other clock groups.
responses.response: I understand the concern about novelty, but I do not think the comb prize covers this step. The comb gives the means to count optical cycles; the lattice clock solves a different problem, how to interrogate many atoms for a long time without trap-induced shifts. That is a new conceptual result, not an improvement of an existing method. I do agree that omitted groups are a real weakness, and I would be glad to hear which part of the lattice-clock record you think is decisive for them.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B031 first as original and lastingly important, ranks B028 third, and stresses that five credited names compete for three places there, so that omitting Esslinger or Cirac is a serious weakness.
responses.response: I share both judgements. B028 is my second choice, but I too find the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Esslinger and Cirac unresolved, and the cold-atom field has already been recognised in 1997 and 2001. B031 has a cleaner attribution and is not tied to an earlier prize, which is why I place it first. If we cannot agree on a trio for B028, I think that should count against it for this year.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery first as an overdue experimental completion of the Standard Model, while acknowledging that choosing three people from two collaborations of thousands is contestable.
responses.response: I accept that the scientific importance of the Higgs discovery is beyond dispute, and I defer to you and Danielsson on particle physics. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: the three credited founders and the spokespeople are not the same set, and committee members have proposed different trios, which suggests the attribution is not settled. I would not call that disqualifying, but it makes B005 harder to defend as a stable configuration than a clean two-person clock prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize to count as a new discovery.
Whether the contributions of Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto, Lemonde and Hinkley change the fair attribution; I have not independently verified the priority history.
I rank B024 sixth and defer to condensed-matter colleagues on its maturity and on the unsettled pairing mechanism.
Whether to prefer a second part, for example B028 or B024, or to keep a single-achievement prize.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups; none of the credited names for B031 (Katori, Ye) is among my collaborators according to my profile, so no specific recusal conflict is apparent for this candidate. I work in the same broad atomic-physics community as the clock and cold-atom candidates (B031, B028), and the committee may wish to note that proximity.
